# Agent Doorbell for Slack

> A small local daemon that watches Slack with your own user token, with no LLM and no tokens spent while quiet, and wakes your AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or any harness) only when a message needs it. MIT licensed, installed with `pipx install agent-doorbell`. Unofficial: not affiliated with Slack, Anthropic or OpenAI.

## What it does

- Watching: a plain Python daemon polls Slack. No LLM, no webhooks, Events API, Socket Mode or public URL, so it works on free Slack workspaces. Matching messages go into per-agent queues; an agent claims items with a 15-minute lease and resolves them with an ack; expired leases redeliver, and after 3 attempts an item is stuck and the owner is notified. Every conversation has a cursor, so after downtime, a reboot or a sleeping laptop it catches up; messages are not missed. With no live agent it is DORMANT: zero Slack API calls. Rate budget: 40 calls a minute per daemon, each conversation polled once. Latency is about 30 seconds.
- Agents: they register themselves (`doorbell register` with a `sub.yaml`). A subscription can say: dms (all, followed, none), group_dms, mentions_of_me, threads_im_in, users, usergroups, channels, everyone_in, allow_bots. `doorbell dispatch` runs one short command per batch. A Claude Code plugin adds skills and hooks that ack automatically. Any agent CLI works with `wait`, `inbox --claim` and `ack`.
- Replying: the daemon never posts. The agent replies with its own Slack tool (for example the Slack MCP, which shows "Sent using @Claude"), or through Doorbell: `doorbell draft` (the owner approves with `doorbell review` and a password), or `doorbell send` and `doorbell react` for agents the owner granted with `doorbell grant` and the password. Direct sends go only into the conversation of one of the agent's own open items, at most 20 an hour by default, and `@channel`, `@here` and `@everyone` become plain text.

## Signing in

`doorbell login` is Slack OAuth with PKCE and a localhost redirect: no client secret, nobody needs to be an app collaborator, the person clicks Allow once, and the token is never shown. Over SSH, open the link on a laptop and paste back the localhost address it ends on, or tunnel the port with `ssh -L 8765:localhost:8765`. Tokens rotate every 12 hours and are renewed automatically (a refresh token lasts 30 days). `doorbell logout` revokes and forgets them. `doorbell status` shows each identity's mode (file or sealed) and status (ok, locked, needs_login, broken).

## The Slack app plan (three layouts)

Doorbell asks for read scopes only, then decides from what the token can really do. A token that can post is never stored in a plain file.

- A. One read-only app: the token is read-only, in a mode-600 file. Unattended, no password, resumes after a restart. Agents cannot send through Doorbell.
- B. One app that allows read and write (single-token mode, `doorbell login --send`): one token watches and sends, sealed with the owner's password. After a restart it is locked until `doorbell unlock`, then catches up. Nothing is missed.
- C. Two apps (a read app and a send app, `doorbell login --send --client-id <send app>`): the watch file stays read-only; the send token is sealed.

Slack adds up the scopes a person approved for one app across all of their tokens for it, until every one is revoked. Approvals are per person. So on one app that allows chat:write, one member can be in A and another in B, and a member who once approved chat:write gets a token that can post, which Doorbell seals or refuses. Admin settings on the app: redirect URL `http://localhost:8765/`, the user token scopes, PKCE on (one-way). "Reinstall to Workspace" grants the installer all configured scopes. The Client ID is not a secret.

## Security model

The password is the boundary for sending. Owner-only commands refuse inside agent sessions. A token that can post never sits in a plain file, and a login-made file token that becomes able to post is revoked and deleted. Credentials files are mode 600. The daemon and the login listener bind 127.0.0.1; the login checks `state`. The daemon never calls an LLM and never writes agent harness settings. Prompt injection is the main risk; limit the agent in its own harness.

## When not to use it

Not for replies within seconds, a team bot everyone @mentions, or setups with no machine of yours running. Only messages are watched, not search, files or canvases.

AI agents helping someone set it up: follow the setup guide, run its check after every step, and never ask for the Slack token in chat (`doorbell login` signs in in the browser; the person clicks Allow).
